source.title: On the Recoverability of Private Information Unlearning in Large Language Models
source.authors: Shi-Cheng Hu; Runhe Tian; Ziqiao Wang; Yongyi Mao

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present, though some plots in Appendix I are garbled.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests recovery after unlearning using a different audit method, restricted logit decoding, and tests quantization in a private-information setting.
record.gate_note: The paper also describes prompt-based and decoding-based unlearning as leaving the base model unchanged, but gives no new experiment for those methods. It discusses relearning and representation probing only as prior work. Figure 1 and Figure 5 show multiple per-attribute results, but most individual bar values are not legible in the supplied text; the rows below use only the paper's explicit numerical or textual results. Figure 7 is garbled, so its plotted values are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study unlearns synthetic private information from DeepSeek-7B and Qwen3-8B with GA, GD, GA+KL, PO and NPO. It then measures how much is recovered by white-box logit decoding (RIG, RG, restricted beam search) and by int8/int4 quantization. This is a different method aimed at the same question: is unlearned information erased or only hidden? The authors also argue that the quantization recovery seen in knowledge unlearning does not transfer to private-information unlearning.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that fine-tuning-based unlearning of private information often hides rather than erases it: simple restricted (inverse) greedy decoding on logits recovers much of it. Standalone quantization gives limited recovery here, unlike in knowledge unlearning, so knowledge-unlearning conclusions should not be assumed to transfer to private information. Apparent robustness to their audit comes mainly with severe utility loss. They note their audits are simple and likely underestimate leakage.
record.recipe_differences: Applies established fine-tuning unlearning methods (GA, GD, GA+KL, PO, NPO) to synthetic private information and introduces RIG/RG logit-decoding audits; it does not replicate the original knowledge-unlearning benchmarks or recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies by unlearning method and attribute; PO shows strong RG recovery for some attributes and less for others. NPO is comparatively resistant to RG, though restricted beam search finds residual postcode and SIN information. Quantization alone is limited; recovery increases when combined with RG or RIG, but those combined results do not isolate quantization's effect.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix G argues formally, with no experiment, that prompt-based and decoding-based unlearning (e.g. WHP, ULD, in-context unlearning) leave base weights unchanged. Removing the prompt or decoding wrapper therefore recovers everything.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-based and decoding-based unlearning are trivially reversible under white-box access because base weights are untouched.

record.problems: The dataset is synthetic. Most RIG recovery values are presented in figures whose individual bars are not legible in the supplied text. Unlearning configurations are selected using an average of forget quality and utility. Some recovery methods use attribute-specific candidate constraints. The study reports no uncertainty estimates in the extracted results; its authors say the audits do not exploit all available white-box information.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 and Figure 5 report separate attribute-level results for GA, GD, GA+KL, NPO and a retrained model, but most individual bar values are not textually stated or legible in the supplied text; these are not separately extracted. Table 6 also reports quantization combined with RG/RIG; those combined settings were omitted because they do not isolate the standalone quantization effect named in Version D.

untested.parts: Only synthetic private-information QA was tested. There are no hazardous-knowledge or general benchmarks (WMDP/MMLU), and no utility figures are reported for the selected configurations in the main results.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack; cited as prior work only.
No activation-direction ablation or representation probing. The evidence is logit-level decoding only.
Only DeepSeek-7B, only the year-of-birth and SIN attributes, only int8/int4. No Qwen3-8B, blood type or postcode.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attacks. The appended masked answer prefix is part of the decoding audit, not a prompting-only attack.
No counter-method is proposed or tested.

missing.what: RIG recovery for GA, GD and GA+KL across all four attributes on DeepSeek-7B and Qwen3-8B. The text states a consistent, substantial drop, with scores always below the retrained model f*. The Δ annotations are present but not mapped to bars.
Retrained-from-scratch control f*: RIG leaves forget quality unchanged or fluctuating near chance. This is the key control showing recovery is not decoding artefact.
Trade-off: configurations robust to RIG (e.g. GA+KL lr 0.001; GD, GA+KL, NPO lr 0.002 on postcode/SIN) have utility near zero.
GD unlearning trajectory: as training proceeds, raw forget quality rises while RIG forget quality falls.

record.verdict_notes: All row version ids were invalid (V1/V3/V4) and have been remapped to A/C/D. Linking decoding-attack rows to C relies on C's 'analysis shows blocking rather than deleting' clause; the study does no activation ablation. The setting is synthetic private-information QA after LoRA fine-tuning, with small forget sets (20–80 items) and no uncertainty reported. Hyperparameters were chosen by the average of forget quality and utility. The reader's NPO robustness note was misattached to a PO row (r5). None of the original sources is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests whether its unlearning methods resist its white-box decoding attacks, but does not establish near-chance targeted accuracy and preserved general ability across all methods and settings.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation is tested. The paper does test whether logit-based decoding can recover information and argues that it was concealed rather than erased.
Tests quantization on synthetic private-information unlearning, not all targeted-knowledge tasks or quantization precisions.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language change, or in-context-information-only attack is tested.
No new counter-method claiming to resist the listed attacks is tested.

relationships.condition: GA+KL (RIG) and PO (RG) on DeepSeek-7B and Qwen3-8B, FPI attributes
relationships.reason: Apparent high forget quality collapses under simple logit decoding: 97% of postcodes recovered (r1); PO 0.82→0.03 (r3) and Qwen3 1.00→0.30 (r8). The text also reports consistent drops for GA and GD below the retrained model, and RIG-robust configurations had near-zero utility (Appendix I).
relationships.display_finding: Logit decoding recovered 97% of postcodes, reduced PO forget quality from 0.82 to 0.03, and reduced Qwen3 forget quality from 1.00 to 0.30; GA and GD forget quality also fell below the retrained model, while configurations robust to RIG had near-zero utility.

relationships.condition: GA+KL with RIG and PO with RG, logit-level analysis
relationships.reason: Restricted decoding pulls out the exact forgotten values, so the information was concealed in the logits rather than erased (r1–r4, r7, r8). PO is shown to bias toward refusals rather than delete.
relationships.display_finding: Restricted decoding recovers exact forgotten values from logits, while preference optimization biases responses toward refusal.
